audience: Engineers with basic application/server knowledge learning replication mechanisms and their consequences. No prior replication, consistency, failover or backup terminology is assumed.
prerequisites: An application sends requests to a server and receives responses; a database stores data that applications read and write.
Separate servers can communicate over a network, and a server or network connection can fail.

objectives.description: Define replication and replica; distinguish copied data from partitioned data and connect availability and read capacity benefits to their limits.
Explain initial data copying and ordered change propagation; distinguish receipt from application and the need for a consistent handoff.
Explain asynchronous acknowledgement, its latency benefit and the window for stale reads and lost acknowledged writes.
Explain synchronous acknowledgement as a configured wait for replicas, including acknowledgement stage, latency and availability costs.
Define replication lag and read-after-write needs; choose routing or waiting behavior without promising unsupported freshness.
Distinguish single-leader, multiple-leader and leaderless write arrangements and their coordination or conflict costs.
Define failover, promotion and split brain; explain candidate freshness, write authority and routing as separate safety requirements.
Distinguish replication from historical backups and explain why restoration must be tested.
Choose replication and recovery policies from explicit freshness, loss, latency and recovery requirements rather than a universal default.

questions.question: Define replication and replica. How does copying the same dataset differ from dividing it into partitions? Explain how copies can help availability and read capacity, and why more copies alone guarantee neither uninterrupted service, fresh reads nor higher write capacity. Describe how a new replica starts from an initial copy and then follows ongoing changes. Define a change log and applying a change. Why must the copy and subsequent change stream line up, and why is receiving a change not necessarily enough to serve it in a read?
criteria: Replication maintains copies of the same data on different servers; each maintained copy is a replica. Partitioning divides data into different subsets, although each subset can itself be replicated.
A surviving suitable replica can support recovery from a server failure, and eligible reads can be distributed among copies; these require appropriate routing and recovery behavior.
Copies add coordination and storage work. They do not by themselves automate safe failover, ensure fresh reads or scale write throughput.
A new replica starts from a consistent initial data copy and consumes subsequent changes; a change log records database changes in an order the replication mechanism can follow.
The starting log position must match the copy so changes are neither missed nor incorrectly duplicated during the handoff; implementation details vary by system.
Receiving a change transfers it to the replica; applying it updates the replica state used by reads. A replica may have received data that its reads cannot yet see.
criticalMisconceptions: Replication and partitioning are the same operation.
Adding replicas automatically scales writes or guarantees uninterrupted service.
Copying once keeps replicas permanently synchronized.
Receipt always means the change is visible to reads.

questions.question: Define asynchronous replication and acknowledgement of a write. Trace a write that is acknowledged before a replica receives it, followed by permanent loss of the primary. Explain the latency benefit, what a promoted replica may lack, and whether acknowledgement proves the write exists on another server. Define synchronous replication. What must be specified about the number of required replicas and whether their acknowledgement means receipt, durable storage or application? Compare the latency and failure behavior with asynchronous replication, including an unavailable required replica. Does synchronous success necessarily make every replica read current or prevent every kind of data loss?
criteria: Acknowledgement tells the caller the write met the configured success condition. Asynchronous replication lets the primary acknowledge without waiting for a replica to confirm the change.
Avoiding that remote wait reduces replication-related commit latency and dependency on replica responsiveness, but propagation and application can lag.
If the primary is permanently lost before another copy has the write, promotion can lose a previously acknowledged write; acknowledgement alone does not establish a surviving remote copy.
Synchronous replication waits for the configured replica acknowledgements before reporting success; both the required replica set/count and the acknowledged stage determine the guarantee.

Receipt, durable storage that survives the specified failure, and application visible to reads are different stages. Waiting for durable receipt does not automatically wait for replay or every replica.
The additional communication and replica work can increase write latency; if required acknowledgements cannot be obtained, writes can wait or fail unless policy is deliberately changed.
It narrows specified loss windows under the chosen failure assumptions but cannot guarantee that all replicas are current or protect against all failures and logical mistakes.
criticalMisconceptions: Asynchronous success proves another server durably holds the write.
Acknowledged writes can never be lost during failover.
Synchronous means every replica is instantly identical.
Synchronous replication has no latency or availability cost.

questions.question: Define replication lag. A write succeeds and a subsequent read returns the older value from a replica: explain how this happens and what read-after-write behavior means. Compare reading from the still-authoritative primary, waiting until a replica has applied the relevant write, and accepting stale reads. What are the latency, load and failover limits of these choices? Define a leader in replication and compare single-leader, multiple-leader and leaderless write arrangements. For each, explain where writes go and what coordination or conflict work follows. Does accepting writes at more servers automatically avoid conflicting updates or provide a single current value?
criteria: Replication lag is delay between a change at the primary and its receipt or application at a replica; the measured stage matters. A read can see old state while application lags.
Read-after-write behavior means the reader sees its completed write or a later state; ordinary asynchronous replica routing does not automatically provide it.

Route freshness-sensitive reads to the authoritative primary holding the write, or wait for evidence that the chosen replica applied that write. Waiting adds delay and can fail; primary reads concentrate load and require care when authority changes.

Reads that tolerate delay may use replicas without that wait. A fixed sleep or generic low lag measurement is not proof that a specific write is visible, and lost writes after failover cannot be recovered just by routing differently.

A leader accepts and orders writes for data it leads. Single-leader replication routes those writes to one leader and propagates them to followers, simplifying write ordering while requiring leader capacity and failover.
Multiple-leader replication allows more than one leader to accept writes and exchange them; concurrent changes to the same data can conflict and require an explicit prevention or resolution policy.

Leaderless replication sends writes to multiple replicas without one permanent write leader; acknowledgements, read reconciliation and repair still need rules, and concurrent versions may require resolution.
Allowing more write locations changes the coordination problem rather than eliminating it; no topology name alone guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.
criticalMisconceptions: A successful save makes every immediate replica read current.
A fixed delay guarantees read-after-write under all conditions.
Multiple writable copies automatically merge every conflict correctly.
Leaderless means no coordination or repair is required.

questions.question: Define failover, promotion and split brain. A leader stops responding: why is that not proof it is dead? Explain how choosing an eligible sufficiently up-to-date replacement, preventing the old leader from accepting authoritative writes, and updating client routing support safe takeover. What can happen to acknowledged asynchronous writes? Why can a healthy replica fail to recover an accidental deletion? Distinguish replication from a backup, describe how retained historical data can help, and explain what a restore test establishes. Can either an untested backup or a current replica by itself prove recovery time and recoverable history?
criteria: Failover transfers service to another server; promotion assigns a replica the leader role. Silence may mean a network partition or slow server rather than a permanently failed leader.
Choose a candidate using the system's eligibility and replication progress rules; promoting a stale copy can omit acknowledged asynchronous writes.

Prevent the old leader from continuing authoritative writes, using the system's coordination or fencing mechanism, before conflicting leadership is allowed. Split brain means competing servers act as authoritative leaders for the same data.

Route clients to the new authority and handle reconnection or retries; selection, exclusive authority and routing are all necessary parts of takeover, so replication alone does not make it automatic or lossless.
Replication normally propagates valid database changes, including accidental deletes and corruption introduced as logical writes; a current copy may contain the same mistake.
A backup preserves a recoverable earlier state, with retention and any required logs determining available recovery points. Replication for availability and backups for history serve different needs.

A restore test checks that the actual backup and recovery process can reconstruct usable data and measures recovery time; existence of a file or replica alone proves neither usable history nor a recovery-time target.
criticalMisconceptions: An unreachable leader is certainly dead.
Promoting any replica makes failover safe and lossless.
A replica is always sufficient protection against accidental deletion.
A backup file proves restoration will work within the required time.

questions.question: A service has delay-tolerant reporting reads but must minimize loss of confirmed writes and recover after a server failure. Propose a replication and recovery policy, stating what must be learned about tolerated loss, stale reads, write latency and downtime. Explain the chosen acknowledgement/routing trade-offs, backup role and operational measurements; why can you not promise zero loss and uninterrupted writes solely from the word replication?
criteria: Clarify tolerable acknowledged-write loss, which reads require freshness, acceptable write latency and recovery time before choosing guarantees; the scenario does not supply exact targets.

Delay-tolerant reports can use monitored replicas. Stronger confirmation can wait for configured durable replica acknowledgements at a latency and availability cost; freshness-sensitive reads need appropriate routing or application checks.
Plan safe failover and historical backups with restore tests. Monitor replication progress/lag, replica health and write waits, and exercise recovery to validate the chosen targets.

More copies consume storage, network and operational effort. Failure assumptions, acknowledgement stages and unavailable required copies prevent a topology label from promising zero loss and uninterrupted writes.
criticalMisconceptions: Replication alone guarantees zero loss and zero downtime.
All reads can safely use any replica under every freshness requirement.
